title: Italiot Greek: Griko of Salento and Greko of Calabria
lead: At the heel and toe of Italy, a few villages still speak Greek. In the Salento, south of Lecce, it is called **γκρίκο** (Griko); in the mountains behind Reggio Calabria, around Bova, it is **γκρέκο** or, in Italian, *grecanico*. Both are written almost always in the Latin alphabet, both are full of Italian and local Romance words, and their speakers are Italian Catholics, not Greeks. Yet a Greek ear catches whole lines: **«Εβώ πάντα σε σένα πενσέω»**, 'I always think of you'. Scholars still argue whether this is the last echo of ancient Magna Graecia or the speech of Byzantine settlers. The answer matters for the whole history of Greek, because it is the one modern dialect, besides Tsakonian, that might not come mainly from the Koine.
facts: **Grecìa Salentina** (Apulia): Calimera, Castrignano dei Greci, Corigliano d'Otranto, Martano, Martignano, Sternatia, Zollino; Melpignano and Soleto belong to the union but have lost the language. **Bovesìa** (Calabria): Bova, Roghudi, Chorio di Roghudi, Roccaforte del Greco, Condofuri, Gallicianò, Amendolea.

Griko: about 20,000, mostly older, with more who understand it. Calabrian Greek: a few hundred active speakers (the Portal's estimate is about 500), all bilingual in a Romance dialect, which is their first language.
Latin alphabet in daily use; Greek script in some publications and song books.
Recognised as a Greek linguistic minority by Italian Law 482 of 1999; listed by UNESCO as endangered.

Debated: continuity from the ancient colonies (Rohlfs, Hatzidakis) or Byzantine resettlement (Morosi, and many Italian scholars). Most specialists now see a Koine-based Byzantine Greek layered on older Doric elements.

sections.h: Three thousand years of Greek in Italy

timeline.text: Greek colonies across the south: **Ρήγιον** (Reggio), **Τάρας** (Taranto), Kroton, Sybaris, Lokroi. The region is called **Μεγάλη Ελλάς**, *Magna Graecia*. Many colonists in the far south spoke Doric.
Roman rule. Latin spreads through the towns, but Greek survives in parts of the countryside and in the Church.

Justinian's reconquest brings southern Italy back under Constantinople. Monks fleeing Iconoclasm and Greeks escaping the Arab conquest of Sicily (9th–10th c.) settle in Calabria and the Salento; the **Catepanate of Italy** is governed from Bari until 1071.
Norman conquest. The Greek rite and Greek monasteries continue for centuries, but the Latin Church gradually replaces them; Bova adopted the Latin rite in 1573.
Two Calabrian Greeks bring Greek back to Western scholarship: **Barlaam of Seminara** teaches Petrarch, and **Leonzio Pilato** translates Homer into Latin for Boccaccio.
Karl Witte 'discovers' Calabrian Greek (1821). Giuseppe Morosi (1870) argues for a Byzantine origin; Gerhard Rohlfs (1924) and Georgios Hatzidakis argue for unbroken continuity from antiquity.
Emigration, poverty, schooling in Italian and stigma shrink both areas. Earthquakes and floods empty old Roghudi; the people move to the coast.
Law 482 recognises the minority. Grecìa Salentina becomes a centre of revival through music and festivals.

sections.h: The great debate: Magna Graecia or Byzantium?
sections.text:
The **Byzantine theory** says that the Greek of southern Italy arrived with settlers from the Peloponnese, Epirus, Central Greece, Euboea and even the Pontus during Byzantine rule. Its strongest argument is that the grammar is plainly medieval Greek, built on the Koine like every other dialect.

The **continuity theory** says that the Greek spoken here never died out after antiquity and was only strengthened by Byzantine monks and refugees. Its strongest argument is a set of **Doric words** found especially in Calabria, some of which are not even attested in the Doric dialects of Greece itself.

Today most scholars, following Horrocks and Fanciullo, combine the two: a medieval Greek whose structure is Koine-based, with older local survivals in the vocabulary.

head: Feature
Italiot
Standard
rows: long or doubled, sometimes with a puff of breath
Retroflex **[ɖ]** (Griko, from λλ, as in local Romance)
**φ** for χ before consonants, **β** for γ

sections.after: The Griko song «Καληνύφτα» shows two of these at once: **νύφτα** for νύχτα and **εβώ** for εγώ. The second is a Griko habit; in Calabria the same word is **εγώ** [eˈgo].

sections.h: Grammar: Greek with an Italian frame
sections.text: The noun has almost lost its case endings. The difference between subject and object is shown mainly by the article, and the genitive is being replaced by prepositional phrases, much as Italian uses *di*. Verbs tend towards one conjugation for all. The aspect difference between imperfect and aorist survives in the past, but in other tenses periphrases do the work, built on the Italian model.
sections.after: That last row is remarkable. Like Pontic Romeyka, Italiot Greek still has a **verb infinitive** where every other dialect uses **να**. It survives mainly after the verb 'can', a relic of medieval Greek kept alive by the Romance infinitive all around it.

Meaning
Standard / source

sections.after: Loans from Italian and the local Romance dialects reach even the closed parts of grammar, such as prepositions, and speakers do not feel them as foreign.

sample.intro: A traditional serenade from Grecìa Salentina, sung today by groups such as Ghetonia. Tap the words.
lines: τσαι που πάω, που σύρνω, που στέω
στην καρδία μου πάντα σένα βαστώ.
en: because I love you, my soul,
and wherever I go, wherever I wander, wherever I stand,
in my heart I always hold you.
sample.source: Traditional; text as given in the Wikipedia article «Griko language».

culture.text: Every August, Melpignano in Grecìa Salentina hosts **La Notte della Taranta**, a huge festival of the *pizzica* tarantella where Griko songs are sung to tens of thousands. Groups such as **Ghetonia** ('neighbourhood', from γειτονιά) and the **Canzoniere Grecanico Salentino** have made Griko songs known abroad, and Calabria has its own festival, **Paleariza** ('old root'). Even the name of the largest Griko town, Calimera, is Greek: **καλημέρα**.

questions.q: In which alphabet is Italiot Greek usually written?
questions.why: Its speakers are schooled in Italian; Greek script appears only in some publications.

questions.q: Which word is the classic evidence for Doric survival in Calabria?
questions.why: It has Doric **α** (λανός) where Attic and the Koine have **η** (ληνός).
A progressive periphrasis modelled on Italian *sto parlando*.

questions.q: What is unusual about «σόζω» + verb in Griko?
questions.why: Standard Greek lost the infinitive; Italiot keeps it after 'can'.
